name: The Dole household
head: dole_george_w

arrival.note: NOT DIRECTLY STATED AND NOT INVENTED EITHER. Andreas's 1833 roster names Dole without an arrival year, which is exactly what the passage does for men already named earlier in the chapter. He is a voter at the first town election of August 1833, which puts him in Chicago before that date under the residence qualification, and the town's own records have him in business here from the start of the decade. 1831 is this project's reading of the earliest year the sources support and it is graded derived; a source that dates his arrival would replace it.

origin.note: NOT ATTESTED IN ANYTHING THIS PROJECT HOLDS. Dole's New England origin and his Detroit connection through Oliver Newberry are widely repeated in the Chicago literature and could not be traced to a source in this dataset, so the value is carried as a conjecture, cites nothing, and is flagged for a later parcel to settle or delete.

reason_for_coming.value: Trade at the head of the lake, in partnership with a Detroit merchant
reason_for_coming.note: The partnership with Oliver Newberry of Detroit is documented in the Democrat and in the bill of lading Andreas prints; a forwarding house at Chicago is the Chicago end of a Detroit business. The MOTIVE is the inference.

lives_at.note: Not attested. Dole's warehouse and packing buildings are in the dataset; his dwelling is not, and no source places him under a roof.

works_at.note: The forwarding and commission house of Newberry & Dole is the firm named in the Democrat of 26 November 1833 and on the schooner Napoleon's bill of lading. This dataset also holds dole_warehouse_south and newberry_dole_slaughterhouse_south_branch under the same partnership; the warehouse is named here as the principal place of business and the others are recorded in this note rather than by inventing a second link.

present_on_scene_date.note: Elected a trustee and treasurer of the town at the July 1835 election.

persons.name: George Washington Dole

occupation.note: Andreas's 1833 roster calls him simply 'George W. Dole, merchant'; the Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 carries the firm 'Newberry & Dole, forwarding and commission merchants'; and the bill of lading Andreas prints for the first cargo of beef, tallow, beeswax and hides ever shipped from Chicago is signed by Newberry & Dole. Forwarding and commission is the more exact trade and is what this record carries.

persons.note: TOWN TREASURER TWICE AND TRUSTEE TWICE - the most continuously documented office-holder in the dataset. Elected trustee 10 August 1833 with 26 of 28 votes (tied top of the poll with Owen), appointed town treasurer at the board's first business meeting on 4 September 1833, and elected trustee AND treasurer again at the third town election of July 1835 (Andreas, scan pp. 273, 369). He is therefore in office on the scene date on the face of the record. Also a provision packer: this dataset holds two slaughtering and packing buildings under his name. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Dole, George W.” (poll_1833_010, line 31); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Dole, George W.” (tax_1833_025, line 77); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Dole, George W.” (poll_1834_034, line 203). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Dole' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “George W. Dole” as treasurer (f1839_r0005, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Dole' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins G. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “DOLE GEORGE W”, 1833-10-22 to 1833-10-24: 4 parcels of the school section — BL73 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL75 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 3 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 6 of block 2 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 9.07 acres stated in all, for $500.50 (ls0147, ls0148, ls0149, ls0150). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: DOLE GEORGE W matches George Washington Dole: the residents layer holds exactly one person of the surname and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.evidence_for: forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'George W. Dole' against resident 'George Washington Dole'

refusals.reason: This card rests on 5 thing(s) the consolidation did not read — andreas_1884_v1, chicago_democrat_1833_11_26, chicago_democrat_1833_1835, fergus_chicago_directory_1839 and others. G2b fired on the seven domains the ladder reads and says nothing about the evidence outside them, so the grade stands. The same reasoning the ladder's own G5 gives for abstaining (T-0515).

research_note: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED BUSINESSMAN IN THE 1835 TOWN and the household that shows what the sources do and do not give. The trade, the partnership, the buildings and the public offices are all attested, some of them contemporaneously. The man's arrival year, his family, his origin and his address are not attested at all. THE NEWBERRY HALF OF THE FIRM IS NOT A CHICAGO HOUSEHOLD: the bill of lading Andreas prints names 'O. Newberry, Detroit', and Andreas describes him throughout as Oliver Newberry of Detroit, builder of the steamer Michigan. He is recorded in data/residents/index.json among the people researched and NOT made residents, which is the honest place for a partner whose home port was the other end of the route.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Dole, George W., city treasurer, Michigan st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `newberry_dole_warehouse`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
